newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/mark steady with traders eyeing new peaks.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/mark steady with traders eyeing new peaks.

text.p: The dollar steadied after hitting a seven-and-a-half-year high against the mark, with traders looking for it to vault above 1.85 marks amid expectations the Bundesbank will not step in anytime soon to curb mark weakness.

The dollar's 5.4 percent surge against the mark so far this month began as a by product of a broad-based weakening in the German unit. This was caused by speculation that a broad group of countries will found European economic and monetary union.
The rally has taken on a life of its own, and the dollar has climbed against other major currencies, as a favourable economic outlook in the U.S. fanned demand for U.S. stocks and bonds.

"At the moment, nothing short of a Bundesbank official being roused from holiday will threaten the dollar's rise," said Nick Parsons, currency strategist at Paribas Capital Markets. "But given the mood the market is in, the dollar will probably go on to test and break 1.85 even if this happens."
The dollar rose to 1.8473 marks, its strongest since November 1989. It also leapt to 1.5250 Swiss francs, its highest since August 1993. Dollar/yen hit a two-month high of 117.42.
Dollar/mark was at 1.8449/54 at 1110 GMT from 1.8354/64 late on Friday in Europe. The U.S. currency was at 117.25/30 yen and at 1.5180/90 Swiss francs from 116.70/80 and 1.5128/38 on Friday.
Bundesbank officials indicated they did not want the mark to weaken further before their summer recess began last week.
Johann Wilhelm Gaddum, vice president of the German central bank, said in an interview last week that the dollar was slightly overvalued.

Also, his fellow council member Reimut Jochimsen said on Friday the Bundesbank, which did not normally allow exchange rates to dictate its policy, was following exchange rates more closely than usual.
Verbal intervention has failed to puncture dollar bullishness, though, analysts said.

"The market does not believe the Bundesbank for a second in terms of its willingness or its ability to support the mark," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
That is because traders do not expect the Bundesbank to intervene or to raise its securities repurchase rate from 3.0 percent anytime soon in the mark's defence.
Talk that the Bundesbank could switch to using variable-rate tenders from the fixed-rate ones it has set since August 1996 proved unfounded last week, encouraging traders to drive the dollar higher.
"It is one thing to talk and another to act," said Parsons at Paribas Capital Markets.

The Bundesbank has retained the option of moving to variable-rate tenders during its summer break by fixing the repo rate for two weeks rather than the usual four weeks. Analysts expect the German central bank to keep its powder dry for as long as possible, though.
"The Bundesbank is unlikely to hike the repo rate unless the dollar is travelling at speed above 1.90," said Mark Geddes, treasury economist at ABN Amro. "This would be a move of last resort."

Such a step may eventually become necessary given that U.S. economic reports later this week are expected to boost U.S. stocks and bonds and the dollar by showing the U.S. economy is expanding without stoking inflation.
Still, with no major economic reports due out of the U.S. until Tuesday's employment cost index and consumer confidence data, traders are looking for the dollar to pause for breath for now.
"It is a technically driven market ahead of tomorrow's data," said a currency trader in London.
-- Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom +44 171 542 6284
